corrections.claimed_speedup: Per WebSearch snippets of cyberscript.dev/performance.html (snippet only): recursive fib (VM) Cyber 19 ms, LuaJIT 21 ms, Luau 34 ms, Lua 39 ms, QuickJS 57 ms (about 2x faster than Lua, derived from page data); fib (JIT) Cyber 5 ms and LuaJIT 5 ms; fiber benchmark Cyber 2.77 +/- 0.28x faster than LuaJIT, 6.28 +/- 0.61x faster than Janet and 8.01 +/- 0.79x faster than Lua; range/iterator (VM) Luau 10 ms, LuaJIT 11 ms, Cyber 12 ms, Lua 27 ms (Cyber slower than Luau and LuaJIT there). The search record's QuickJS 78 ms range figure did not reappear in the snippets this verifier saw.
corrections.caveats: Snippet only: cyberscript.dev is blocked here, so hardware, compiler flags and the Lua, LuaJIT, Luau, QuickJS and Janet versions were not seen. The benchmark sources the examples/README links (test/bench) were removed from master, but they exist at tag 0.3 (Dec 2023): test/bench/fib, fiber, for, heap and string with .cy, .lua, .luau and .js versions (fib also C, Go, Java and others); the 0.3 fiber directory has no Janet file, so the Janet comparison was run on code not present at that tag. The last numbered release is 0.3 (Dec 2023); master has been heavily reworked since, so the published numbers probably describe the 0.3-era VM and JIT rather than current master. notes: Fib and fiber numbers confirmed through two WebSearch snippets of the blocked performance page. Benchmark code is at https://github.com/fubark/cyber/tree/0.3/test/bench, not on master. tier_reason: The README table compares qjsc -A with a base QuickJS interpreter commit on the V8 v7/v9 suites on a Mac M4 (Debian 13 VM), median of 20 runs, but the harness and benchmark sources are not in the repo or linked from it, and the clang version is not stated. That makes it first-party with partial methodology: C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: qjsc -A (each bytecode function compiled to C by unrolling the interpreter loop) scores 3518 vs 2582 for the base QuickJS interpreter on the v8-v7 geomean (about 1.36x, derived from page data) and 7784 vs 5425 on v8-v9 (about 1.43x, derived). The best individual cases are about 2.1x (derived): NavierStokes 7946 vs 3710, Crypto 4305 vs 2018, MandreelLatency 33458 vs 16673 and Mandreel 3973 vs 1957; RegExp gains only about 4% and CodeLoad none. Each printed % column is the next column relative to the previous one: the tail-call dispatch branch alone is +8.45% (v8-v7, 2800) and +13.29% (v8-v9, 6146) over base, and qjsc -A is +25.64% and +26.65% over tail-call dispatch.
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers with incomplete methodology: the clang version, the build flags of the base interpreter and the benchmark harness are not documented in the README, and the repo has no V8 benchmark files (tests/ holds only microbench.js and the test suites). The author's separate ivankra/javascript-zoo repo has a bench/ directory with V8-suite scripts (v8-v7.js, richards.js and others) and bench.py, which is probably the harness, but the README does not link it. The baseline is the author's own QuickJS fork commit b226856, not an upstream bellard/quickjs release. Gains depend on the workload (RegExp +4%, CodeLoad none) and the author calls the result modest; the project is a proof of concept. GitHub shows no fork link to bellard/quickjs, although the code and LICENSE (MIT, Bellard and Gordon) are QuickJS's.

notes: The headline numbers match the README. The search record misread the % columns: they are column-to-column ratios, so tail-call dispatch is +8.45% and +13.29% over base and AOT is about +26% over tail. The best case is NavierStokes at 2.14x (derived), not Crypto. MIT confirmed from the LICENSE file; last commit 2025-12-09; 9 stars; default branch aot.

tier_reason: The README's 59 KB vs 136 KB memory figures come from ARCHITECTURE.md section 1.3 'Memory Targets', a pre-implementation spec ('Status: Ready for Implementation') that adds up per-component estimates for a hypothetical 50 KB app. The ~170 KB size matches the spec's ~166 KB binary budget. bench/bench_runner.c, which the Makefile's bench target needs, does not exist (404). Nothing measures r8e against QuickJS, so it is D.

corrections.claimed_speedup: No measured claim. The README's 'Key Properties' table lists runtime memory 59 KB vs 136 KB for QuickJS on a 50 KB app and a binary size of about 170 KB vs about 1.5 MB for QuickJS. These figures are design targets copied from ARCHITECTURE.md section 1.3 'Memory Targets' (component estimates: parse peak, object, string, closure, bytecode and GC metadata), not results from running either engine. There is no speed claim: the spec's own goal is to reach 80% of QuickJS performance at 50% of the memory.
corrections.caveats: Not a measurement: the memory and size numbers are pre-implementation targets from ARCHITECTURE.md (Version 1.0 spec, 'Status: Ready for Implementation'); the QuickJS column is also an estimate. The README lists a bench/ directory and the Makefile builds bench/bench_runner.c, but the repo has no bench/ directory (bench_runner.c returns 404), so 'make bench' cannot run. CI only reports the size of the static archive libr8e.a and warns above 200 KB. The 1.5 MB QuickJS binary figure has no stated source and looks like a full CLI build. Very young repo (31 commits from 2026-03-05 to 2026-03-26, 1 star), written with heavy AI assistance (CLAUDE.md lists agent tasks), with recent commits still fixing basic engine test failures. It is slower than QuickJS by design (plain interpreter, target 80% of QuickJS speed).
corrections.workload: Projected memory for a hypothetical 50 KB JavaScript app (200 objects, 500 strings, 100 closures) and a target binary size, from the README table and ARCHITECTURE.md section 1.3; no workload was actually run.

notes: Downgraded C to D: the README numbers are spec targets presented as properties, with no benchmark code (bench/ is missing) and no measured comparison. Under the keep-and-document rule this is a downgrade, not a reject. If the orchestrator treats projected numbers presented as results as invalid evidence (like the hard-coded baseline precedent), a reject is defensible. Not notable (1 star). Metadata (MIT, last commit 2026-03-26, active, not a fork) checked on github.com.
